clinician.final_diagnosis: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) with ectopic ACTH production (Cushing's syndrome) and superior vena cava syndrome
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 56-year-old Asian male smoker (>25 pack-years) presented with a 3-month history of progressive respiratory distress, proximal muscle weakness, hyperpigmentation, significant weight loss (10 kg), and apathy. Clinical examination revealed prominent upper body swelling with skin plethora, prominent neck and upper body veins, hyperpigmentation of face and hands, cachectic appearance (BMI 18.1 kg/m²), severe hypertension (180/100 mm Hg), moderate respiratory distress, and reduced proximal muscle power in all four limbs. Chest imaging (X-ray and CT) identified a right hilar mass (11.7×5.7×4.7 cm) with severely stretched proximal superior vena cava showing luminal narrowing, confirming superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) and staging the disease as T4N2M0 (stage IIIb). Laboratory investigations revealed severe hypokalaemia (refractory to IV KCl infusion), hyperglycaemia, and mild hypocalcaemia. Endocrine workup showed raised 9-am serum cortisol with increased ACTH levels, indicating ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism. Notably, cortisol remained unsuppressed despite high-dose dexamethasone (2 days prior to testing), confirming ectopic ACTH secretion. Bronchial biopsy histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of small cell lung cancer. The patient was initiated on urgent chemotherapy with etoposide (120 mg daily IV for 5 days) and cisplatin (70 mg IV on day 1), along with supportive care including spironolactone and IV KCl for hypokalaemia, ketoconazole for steroidogenesis inhibition, and prophylactic antibiotics. The SVCS responded rapidly to treatment with complete reduction of upper body edema and resolution of respiratory distress within 5 days.
